author: Jordan Blum
title: EOG Resources touts $2.4 billion quarterly profit driven by tax law - Houston Chronicle
text:
window._taboola = window._taboola || []; _taboola.push({ mode: 'thumbnails-c', container: 'taboola-interstitial-gallery-thumbnails-4', placement: 'Interstitial Gallery Thumbnails 4', target_type: 'mix' }); _taboola.push({flush: true}); Image 1 of / 4 4 Image 2 of 4 Image 3 of 4 Image 4 of 4 EOG Resources touts $2.4 billion quarterly profit driven by tax law 1 / 4 Back to Gallery Houston's EOG Resources reported a big $2.4 billion quarterly profit that's largely derived from a roughly $2 billion, one-time benefit from the new U.S. tax law.
The big profit - still about $400 million without the assist from the tax law - compares favorably to a $142 million loss during the fourth quarter of 2016. EOG's quarterly revenues jumped almost 40 percent from last year up to $3.34 billion.
As such, EOG is increasing its dividend payouts to investors by more than 10 percent and potentially hiking its capital spending by more than 40 percent in 2018.
The massive tax windfall primarily comes from the revaluations of deferred taxes and existing U.S.assets.
Recommended Video: Now Playing: EU state regulators are to investigate whether Swedish furniture retailer Ikea's tax arrangement with the Netherlands helped cut its tax bill. The European Commission says it is looking into two tax rulings issued to Inter Ikea, which operates Ikea's franchise business and collects a fee of three percent of turnover from all Ikea shops via a subsidiary - Inter Ikea Systems - in the Netherlands. What is the Commission saying? That the first tax ruling, which covered 2006 to 2011, resulted in a significant part of Inter Ikea Systems' franchise profits shifting to a Luxembourg unit where it was not taxed. A 2011 ruling, broght in after the Commission declared the first deal illegal, allowed a substantial part of the company's franchise profits after 2011 to be transferred to its Liechtenstein plant. Analysts say it is the latest crackdown on unfair tax deals between multinationals and EU countries. Has Inter Ikea said anything? Yes. Inter Ikea said it and Inter Ikea Systems are committed to paying ta in line with the laws of the countries in which they operate. The company says it believes the way it has been taxed is in accordance with EU rules. Are any other companies in the frame? Yes. Fast-food chain McDonald's (MCD.N) and French energy company Engie (ENGIE.PA) are also in the EU's crosshairs over their Luxembourg tax deals. The Commission has already cracked down on some companies, hasn't it? Yes. They have ordered: - Apple (AAPL.O) to pay a record amount of back taxes, 13 billion euros to Ireland. - Starbucks (SBUX.O) to pay up to 30 million euros to the Netherlands - Amazon (AMZN.O) to pay 250 million euros to Luxembourg. - Belgium has been told to recover a total of 700 million euros from 35 firms, including Anheuser-Busch InBev (ABI.BR), BP (BP.L) and BASF (BASFn.DE) because of an illegal tax scheme. Last month, the Commission launched an investigation into a British tax exemption for multinational companies set up in 2013 by the then-Conservative-led government to attract companies to set up headquarters in Britain. What they are saying "All companies, big or small, multinational or not, should pay their fair share of tax. Member states cannot let selected companies pay less tax by allowing them to artificially shift their profits elsewhere," - European Competition Commissioner Margrethe Vestager.
Media: Euronews "EOG emerged from the industry downturn in 2017 with unprecedented levels of efficiency and productivity, driving oil production volumes to record levels with capital expenditures approximately one half the prior peak," said EOG CEO Bill Thomas.
Higher oil prices, increased production volumes and improved efficiencies also drove profits, he said.
RELATED: EOG banks first profit in nearly two years; pumps record oil
Driven by growth in West Texas' booming Permian Basin and its large position in South Texas, the oil and gas producer saw its oil production volumes jump 20 percent last year. EOG was considered a pioneer a few years back in the Eagle Ford and continues to produce heavily there, although most of the industry focus has pivoted to the Permian.
EOG counts an inventory of thousands of premium wells that were previously drilled but are yet to be completed to start producing oil.
To take advantage of those wells, EOG said it will increase its 2018 capital spending from about $4.1 billion last year to a range of $5.4 billion to $5.8 billion. Thomas said EOG only needs oil priced at about $50 a barrel to see those plans successfully executed and U.S. oil prices currently are hovering above $62 per barrel.
Apart from the Texas plays, EOG also plans to increase its spending in Colorado, Oklahoma and North Dakota shale acreage.
EOG is hiking its quarterly dividend payouts for the first time in four years from 16.8 cents a share to 18.5 cents per share - an increase of more than 10 percent.
Elsewhere in Texas, EOG said it's continuing to test its position in South Texas' Austin Chalk, a geologically complex formation that lies above the Eagle Ford.
